title: The phone that never rang
dek: Waiting for a call from your own child is a grief with no funeral and no end date.
body: Every day, I check my phone. Not because I am waiting for work. Not because I am expecting important news. I am waiting for my child.
One call. One text. Even one simple message saying: “Dad, how are you?”
The hardest part is not that the phone stays silent. The hardest part is that I still remember the sound of that little voice.
I remember bedtime stories. I remember scraped knees. I remember carrying them on my shoulders. And now I am staring at a screen that has nothing on it.
Child estrangement creates a strange kind of grief. The person you love is still alive. Somewhere. Growing. Laughing. Living. But you no longer know what is happening in their life.
And still, you wait. Not because you are weak. Because love does not always disappear when contact does.
q: What is something you still wait to hear from someone you love?

title: “I didn’t know what to say”
dek: Sometimes silence isn’t indifference. Sometimes it’s the hundredth attempt going unanswered.
body: Sometimes a father doesn’t reach out because he doesn’t care. Sometimes he doesn’t reach out because he has already reached out a hundred times.
The birthday cards. The messages. The phone calls. The apologies. The invitations. Eventually silence begins to feel safer than another rejection.
But silence gets misunderstood. A child may think: “He stopped trying.” And the father is sitting alone thinking: “I don’t know how to reach you anymore.”

That is one of the painful realities of family separation. Two people can love each other. Two people can miss each other. And they can still be separated by silence, misunderstanding, hurt, fear, or circumstances neither knows how to repair.
Sometimes the first step toward healing is not knowing exactly what to say. Sometimes it is simply being willing to say: “I am here when you are ready.”
q: Have you ever had words you wanted to say but were afraid to send? What stopped you?

title: The empty chair
dek: An empty chair stops being furniture and becomes a statement.
body: There was always a chair for them. At dinner. At Christmas. At birthdays. For years nobody said anything about it. We just left the space.
One day someone finally asked me: “Why do you keep setting that place?” I looked down and said: “Because this is still home.”

Estrangement changes the way you experience ordinary things. An empty chair is no longer just a chair. A birthday is no longer just a celebration. A holiday is no longer just a holiday. Everything becomes a reminder.
And sometimes the people around you don’t understand why you are still grieving. But missing your child does not have an expiration date. Love does not follow the rules of distance.
q: Is there a place, object, song, or tradition that reminds you of someone you miss?

title: When a child starts speaking differently
dek: The words sound borrowed. Several things can be true at once.
body: One day the words sounded unfamiliar. The phrases. The accusations. The way my child spoke. I listened and quietly thought: “That doesn’t sound like you.”
In high-conflict family situations, parents sometimes feel that a child’s language, beliefs, or feelings have been heavily influenced by the adults around them.
But family relationships are rarely simple. Children can have real feelings. Parents can make mistakes. Influence can exist. Hurt can exist. Sometimes several of those are true at once.
That is why this site believes in listening before judging. No child’s voice should be dismissed. And no parent’s pain should be mocked or ignored by default.
Healing begins when people are allowed to speak honestly about complicated relationships.
q: Have you ever heard words from someone you love that changed everything between you?

title: The birthday card
dek: I still buy the card every year, and I never know if it is opened.
body: I still buy the card. Every year. I stand in the store longer than I need to, reading every message. Too cheerful. Too formal. Too emotional.
Eventually I find one. Then I write: “Happy Birthday. I love you. Dad.” Nothing dramatic. Nothing demanding. Just proof that somewhere, someone remembered.
Maybe the card gets opened. Maybe it doesn’t. Maybe it goes in the bin. Maybe it sits in a drawer. I don’t know. I send it anyway.
Because sometimes love is not about knowing how your message will be received. Sometimes it is simply about leaving a door open.
q: If you could send one sentence to someone you miss, what would it say?

title: Father’s Day
dek: For some fathers it is breakfast in bed. For others it is a day to survive.
body: Father’s Day can be complicated. For some fathers, it is breakfast in bed. Cards. Phone calls. Laughter.

For others, it is a day they quietly try to survive. They see photographs of other families. They scroll past messages saying: “Happy Father’s Day to the best dad!” And somewhere inside, a question appears: “Does my child even remember me?”
If Father’s Day is painful for you, you are allowed to admit it. You don’t have to pretend. You don’t have to turn pain into a motivational quote.
You can simply say: “Today is hard.” And that is enough.
q: What does Father’s Day mean to you now?

title: The story nobody asked me about
dek: People heard one version. That became the story.
body: People heard one version of the story. And that became the story.

Nobody asked me what happened. Nobody asked what I lost. Nobody asked what I regretted. Nobody asked what I wished I could change. They simply decided who I was. A bad father. An absent father. A father who didn’t care.

But people are more complicated than a sentence. Some fathers have made serious mistakes. Some have been misunderstood. Some have been pushed out. Some have lived through manipulation or conflict. Some are carrying regret and grief at the same time.
Accountability matters. Truth matters. So does listening.
q: Have you ever felt judged by people who never knew the full story?

title: “I’m sorry”
dek: An apology doesn’t fix everything. It can still be the beginning.
body: Sometimes the hardest letter begins with two words. I’m sorry.
Not because saying sorry fixes everything. It doesn’t. Not because an apology guarantees reconciliation. It doesn’t.

But sometimes healing begins when we stop defending every mistake we made. A father may look back and realize: “I could have done better.” That realization can hurt. But it can also be the beginning of growth.
There is courage in taking responsibility. There is strength in saying: “I didn’t understand then what I understand now.” An apology is not weakness. When it is sincere, it can be an act of love.
q: Is there something you wish you could apologize for — or something you wish someone would apologize to you for?

title: Grief without a funeral
dek: Ambiguous loss is still loss.
body: Estrangement can feel like grief without a funeral. There is no day when everyone gathers. No final goodbye. No clear ending.
Instead, there are questions. Are they okay? Do they remember me? Will they ever call? Will we speak again?
The uncertainty can be exhausting. And because the person is still alive, other people may not understand why you are grieving.
But ambiguous loss is still loss. You can miss someone who is still somewhere in the world. You can love someone from a distance. You can hope and hurt at the same time.
q: What is the hardest part of living with unanswered questions?

title: The message I never sent
dek: Silence becomes a prison built out of fear.
body: I typed it. Deleted it. Typed it again. Deleted it again.
Finally I wrote: “I don’t know if you want to hear from me. I don’t want to pressure you. I just want you to know that I think about you.” I stared at the screen. Then I put the phone down.

Estranged parents are not usually silent because they have nothing to say. They are silent because they are terrified of saying the wrong thing. What if I make it worse? What if they don’t respond? What if they tell me never to contact them again?
Silence becomes a prison built out of fear.
q: Have you ever written a message and deleted it? What did you want to say?

title: When people say “just move on”
dek: As if love were a light switch.
body: “Just move on.” As if love were a light switch. As if you could simply wake up one morning and decide that your child no longer mattered.

Moving forward does not have to mean forgetting. Healing does not require erasing. You can build a meaningful life and still miss someone. You can laugh again and still carry grief. You can have hope without putting your entire life on hold.
Maybe the goal is not to “move on.” Maybe the goal is to learn how to move with the pain — without letting it destroy you.
q: What does healing look like to you?

title: The grandchild he has never met
dek: Losing a child can mean losing the generation after them.
body: There are forms of distance that are difficult to explain. A father can lose contact with a child. And sometimes, through that separation, lose contact with grandchildren too.
Birthdays happen. First steps happen. School begins. Life moves forward. And the grandparent watches from far away — or not at all.
This kind of separation can feel like missing chapters from a book you desperately wanted to read.
Yet love can still exist without photographs. Without visits. Without knowing someone’s favorite color. Sometimes love waits. Quietly. Patiently.
q: Have family conflicts ever caused you to miss important moments you can never get back?

title: The anger under the sadness
dek: Anger is human. What we do with it matters.
body: Not every day is sadness. Sometimes it is anger. Anger at the situation. Anger at decisions. Anger at lost years. Anger at yourself. Anger at the people you believe contributed to the distance.
Anger is a human emotion. But what we do with anger matters. If we let it control every conversation, it can deepen the very distance we want to heal.
Sometimes healing means finding a safe place to say: “I am angry.” Without turning that anger into destruction.
Write. Pray. Talk to someone you trust. Seek professional support when needed. Feel the emotion. But don’t let it write the entire story of your life.
q: What helps you when anger begins taking over your thoughts?

title: The photograph
dek: How do two people in one photograph become strangers?
body: I found the photograph in an old box. There we were. Smiling. Younger. Happy. For a moment I couldn’t breathe.
How do two people in one photograph become strangers?

Family separation leaves you searching through memories, trying to find the exact moment everything changed. But sometimes there was no single moment. Sometimes a relationship breaks slowly, under years of misunderstanding, conflict, communication failures, outside influence, or pain nobody resolved.
Looking backward hurts. Sometimes it also teaches you something about going forward.
q: Do you ever look at old photographs? How do they make you feel?

title: A letter to my child
dek: I don’t know when we will speak again. I remember you anyway.
body: Dear Child,
I don’t know where life will take us. I don’t know when we will speak again. I don’t know if you are angry, hurt, confused, or simply trying to live your life.
But I want you to know this. I remember you. I remember the little things. The things nobody else would remember.
And wherever life takes us, there will always be a part of me that hopes you are safe, healthy, and happy.
I am still learning. I am still growing. And I am still here.
Love, Dad.
q: If you could write the first line of a letter to someone you miss, what would it be?

title: The things we don’t say to men
dek: Who does a grieving father tell?
body: Men are often taught to be strong. Keep going. Don’t cry. Don’t complain. Handle it.
But what happens when a father is grieving the loss of a relationship with his child? Who does he tell? Where does he go? How does he explain why he suddenly becomes quiet during family holidays?

Strength does not mean pretending you are not hurting. Sometimes strength is saying: “I’m not okay today.” Sometimes strength is asking for help. Sometimes strength is crying in a room where you finally feel safe.
Dads need spaces to speak too.
q: Do you believe fathers are given enough space to talk about emotional pain? Why or why not?

title: Hope without a guarantee
dek: Hope can hurt. It may need a different definition.
body: Hope can be difficult. Because hope can hurt. Every time the phone rings, you wonder. Every birthday, you wonder. Every holiday, you wonder. “Maybe this will be the year.”
But reconciliation cannot always be promised. And false promises can be harmful. So perhaps hope needs a different definition.
Hope can mean: I will continue growing. I will continue healing. I will remain open to healthy communication. I will respect boundaries. I will not stop becoming a better version of myself.
Hope is not always waiting for someone else to change. Sometimes hope is continuing to live.
q: What does hope mean to you when you don’t know what the future holds?

title: When your child blocks you
dek: How do you love someone and give them space at the same time?
body: There is something painful about seeing that you can no longer reach someone. A blocked number. A blocked account. A message that will never be delivered. It can feel final.
But a blocked door does not always tell you everything about the future. At the same time, respecting boundaries matters. Repeatedly forcing contact can sometimes cause more harm.

This is where emotional maturity becomes difficult. How do you love someone and give them space? How do you hope without chasing? How do you remain present without forcing your way into someone’s life?
There may not be one answer. But these are conversations worth having.
q: Have you ever struggled to balance reaching out with respecting someone’s boundaries?

title: Lost time
dek: Time cannot be replaced. Tomorrow can still be built.
body: One of the deepest pains of estrangement is time. The birthdays you missed. The graduations. The ordinary afternoons. The conversations that never happened.
Time can feel stolen. And unlike money or possessions, time cannot simply be replaced. That grief is real.
But if a door ever opens again, the future does not have to be identical to the past. You cannot recover yesterday. But you may still be able to create a new tomorrow.
And while you wait, your own life still deserves care.
q: If you could recover one ordinary day with someone you miss, what would you do differently?

title: The prayer
dek: A place to put the things you cannot control.
body: Some people pray for reconciliation. Not for victory. Not to prove someone wrong. But for healing.
For understanding. For wisdom. For softened hearts. For the courage to admit mistakes. For the strength to forgive. For peace, even when reconciliation does not happen quickly.
Prayer can be a place to put the things you cannot control. A place to release the questions that have no immediate answers.
q: If you pray, what is one thing you are praying for today?

title: When someone uses a child as a weapon
dek: The child should never have to become the battlefield.
body: In some high-conflict family situations, children may become caught between adults. They may hear negative things. Feel pressure to choose sides. Feel responsible for someone else’s emotions. Or become involved in conflicts they did not create.
This can be painful for everyone — including the child.
Children deserve the freedom to have their own feelings. They deserve safety. They deserve to love without feeling forced to choose.
When adults are hurting, it can be difficult not to turn the child into the battlefield. But the child should never have to become the battlefield.
q: What do you believe children need most when adults are in conflict?

title: I saw them from across the room
dek: I wanted to walk over. I didn’t know if I was welcome.
body: I saw them. Across the room. Older now. Different haircut. Different clothes. I knew immediately.
For a second everything else disappeared. The noise. The people. The years. I wanted to walk over. To hug them. To say: “Look at you.”
Instead I stood still. Because I didn’t know if I was welcome.
Estrangement creates impossible moments. You want to reach out, and you are afraid of making it worse. You want to respect their space, and every part of you wants to say their name.
q: What would you say if you unexpectedly had one peaceful minute with someone you miss?

title: The power of one apology
dek: “I’m sorry you feel that way” is not an apology.
body: An apology cannot rewrite history. But it can acknowledge it.
A meaningful apology does not say: “I’m sorry you feel that way.” It says: “I understand that my actions hurt you.”
It doesn’t demand forgiveness. It doesn’t make excuses. It doesn’t keep score.
Sometimes reconciliation begins with accountability. And sometimes an apology is part of healing even when reconciliation doesn’t happen.
q: Do you believe a sincere apology can change a relationship? Why or why not?

title: You are still a parent
dek: Estrangement can make someone question their identity.
body: Estrangement can make someone question their identity. If my child doesn’t call me — am I still a dad? If I wasn’t invited — am I still a mom?
Parenthood is complicated. Relationships can change. Roles can change. Contact can disappear.
But the memories, responsibilities, love, regrets, and experiences that shaped you do not simply vanish.
You may need to redefine what parenthood means in this season of your life. But you are still allowed to acknowledge your story.
q: How has estrangement or family distance changed the way you see yourself as a parent?

title: The friend who finally listened
dek: Sometimes you don’t need answers. You need a witness.
body: I didn’t need advice. I didn’t need someone to tell me to move on. I didn’t need someone to explain my own life to me. I needed someone to listen.
One friend finally said: “Tell me about your child.” And for the first time in years, I did.
Sometimes healing begins with a simple question. Sometimes you don’t need answers — you need a witness. Someone willing to sit beside you in the uncomfortable part of your life.
q: Who has been a safe person for you during a difficult season?

title: You can miss them and still live
dek: Healing is not abandonment.
body: Healing does not mean forgetting. It does not mean giving up. It does not mean loving your child less. It means remembering that your life is still happening too.
Eat. Sleep. Laugh. Build friendships. Create. Travel. Pray. Get help. Find purpose.

You are allowed to experience joy without betraying the person you miss. Sometimes people feel guilty when they begin feeling better. But healing is not abandonment. Taking care of yourself does not mean you have stopped loving them.
q: What is one small thing you are doing to take care of yourself right now?

title: If my child ever reads this
dek: I hope we can walk through it slowly. One conversation at a time.
body: If you ever read this, I want you to know I have spent a lot of time thinking. About what happened. About what I could have done differently. About the things I wish I understood sooner.
I don’t expect this letter to fix everything. I don’t expect you to forget your pain.
I simply want you to know that beneath all the years, silence, questions, and distance, there is still love.
And if a healthy door ever opens, I hope we can walk through it slowly. One conversation at a time.
q: What does a healthy first conversation after years of silence look like to you?

title: The community we need
dek: A place where nobody has to explain why they are hurting.
body: Imagine a place where nobody has to explain why they are hurting. Where someone can write: “Today was hard.” And someone else understands.

Where a father can admit: “I miss my daughter.” And nobody laughs. Where a mother can say: “I don’t know what I did wrong.” And nobody rushes to judge. Where an adult child can share their perspective. And people listen.
That is the kind of community we want to build. Not a place for hate. Not a place to attack former partners. Not a place to decide who is right without knowing the story.
A place for truth. Reflection. Accountability. Compassion. And hope.
q: What would make you feel safe in an online community like this?

title: Still loving them
dek: The human heart can hold complicated things.
body: Maybe nobody sees it. The way you remember. The way you worry. The way you wonder where they are. The way you quietly hope your name might appear on their phone one day.
Maybe they don’t know. Maybe they do. But love can survive long periods of silence.
That does not mean every relationship will return. It does not mean we should ignore boundaries or avoid accountability. It simply means the human heart can hold complicated things.
Pain and hope. Regret and love. Grief and gratitude. Distance and memory.
q: Who are you still loving from a distance?

title: You found us for a reason
dek: Sometimes the most powerful thing you can hear is: me too.
body: Maybe you were searching for answers. Maybe you were searching for the words estranged father. Maybe parental alienation. Maybe I miss my child. Or maybe you weren’t searching for anything. Maybe this post simply appeared.
Whatever brought you here, we are glad you found us.

Dad, Still Here is more than a channel. We hope it becomes a place where people can tell the truth about family distance. Where anonymous letters can carry the words people have held inside for years. Where fathers can speak. Where mothers can speak. Where adult children can be heard. Where healing is not rushed. Where accountability is respected. Where hope is allowed.
Because sometimes the most powerful thing you can hear is: “Me too.” And suddenly, you realize you are not alone.
q: What is one thing you wish people understood about the pain of being separated or estranged from someone you love?

title: The first snow
dek: Some seasons arrive carrying a person with them.
body: The first snow came early this year. I stood at the window longer than I meant to.
Years ago that was the morning we went looking for the sled in the garage. Wet gloves on the radiator. Hot chocolate nobody finished.
Estrangement does this. It hides inside ordinary weather and waits for you.
I used to fight those memories. Now I let them sit with me for a minute, the way you let an old friend in from the cold.
They still hurt. They also remind me that it was real. We were a family who went looking for the sled.
q: Is there a season or a kind of weather that brings someone back to you?

title: The voicemail I saved
dek: Eleven seconds I have listened to more times than I can count.
body: There is a voicemail on my phone from years ago. Eleven seconds. “Hi Dad, call me back.”
I have changed phones twice. Each time, the first thing I did was make sure it came with me.
It isn’t an important message. That is what makes it precious. It was just an ordinary day when calling me back was a normal thing to ask.
Some people would tell me to delete it. That holding on keeps the wound open.
Maybe. But some days that voice is the proof I need that we were once easy with each other. And if it happened once, it is not impossible.
q: Is there something small you have kept because it holds someone’s voice?

title: What I tell people at work
dek: “Do you have kids?” is a harder question than it sounds.
body: A new colleague asked me the other day if I had kids. Everyone asks eventually. It is a kind question.
I said yes. Then came the next one: “How old? What are they up to?” And I didn’t know.
I have a few answers ready now. Sometimes I say, “It’s complicated.” Sometimes I just give an age and change the subject.
Neither answer feels honest. Neither feels like a lie. Estranged parents learn to live in that in-between space every day.
If you have ever fumbled that question, you are not alone. You don’t owe anyone the whole story. You are allowed to protect the tender places.
q: How do you answer when people ask about your family?

title: The long way home
dek: I still drive past the school.
body: There is a shorter route home. I don’t take it.
I take the one that goes past the old school. The gate is painted a different color now. The crossing guard I used to wave to retired years ago.
I know it doesn’t change anything. I know my child isn’t there anymore. I still slow down.
Grief makes us loyal to places. They are the only part of the past we can still visit.
I am not stuck. I am just taking the long way, for a little while longer.
q: Is there a place you still visit because of someone you miss?

title: Learning to listen
dek: Being heard and being right are not the same thing.
body: For a long time, every time I imagined us talking again, I imagined explaining myself.
My side. My reasons. The things I thought had been misunderstood.
Somewhere along the way I realized that if the door ever opens, I don’t want to walk in arguing.
I want to listen. Even to the parts that are hard to hear. Even to the parts I remember differently.
Listening isn’t agreeing. It is saying: your experience mattered to me then, and it matters to me now. That might be the most loving thing a father can practice while he waits.
q: What helps you listen when what you hear is painful?

title: The holidays are coming
dek: The season of togetherness can be the loneliest time of year.
body: The decorations are going up in the shops already. Songs about coming home are playing everywhere.
For many estranged parents, the holidays are not a celebration. They are something to get through.
The empty seat feels louder. The phone feels quieter. Everyone else’s photographs feel brighter.
If that is you, plan for it now. Decide where you will be. Decide who you will call. Give yourself permission to do things differently this year.
You don’t have to pretend it’s fine. You just have to get through it gently. And you won’t be the only one doing that.
q: What is one thing that makes the holidays a little easier for you?

title: I used to be the fixer
dek: Some things can’t be fixed by trying harder.
body: I have always been the one who fixes things. Leaky taps. Flat tires. Problems at work.
So when my child stopped speaking to me, I did what I always do. I tried to fix it.
More messages. Better words. The right gift at the right time. Each attempt was a tool I thought would work.
It took me a long time to learn that a relationship isn’t a machine. You can’t force it back together.
Now I am learning a different skill. Patience. Steadiness. Being the kind of man who would be safe to come back to. It’s the hardest repair job I have ever taken on.
q: Have you ever had to stop trying to fix something and simply wait?

title: The song on the radio
dek: Three minutes that can undo a whole day.
body: I was in the supermarket when it came on. A silly song we used to sing in the car, loud and badly, with the windows down.
I had to leave my trolley in the aisle and stand outside for a while.
People don’t warn you about this part. Grief doesn’t only arrive on anniversaries. It ambushes you next to the cereal.
I used to feel embarrassed by moments like that. Now I think they are just love with nowhere to go.
I went back in and finished the shopping. I hummed the rest of the song on the way home.
q: Is there a song that takes you straight back to someone?

title: What I would do differently
dek: Regret can become a teacher instead of a sentence.
body: I think about the things I would do differently. I won’t pretend there aren’t any.
I would listen more and lecture less. I would say sorry faster. I would put the phone down at dinner.
For a while, those thoughts were a punishment I replayed every night.
Now I try to let them teach me instead. I can’t change who I was then. I can change who I am now.
Regret that changes nothing is just pain. Regret that changes how you live might one day become a bridge.
q: What is something you have learned about yourself through a painful season?

title: The other parent
dek: Bitterness keeps you tied to the past.
body: It is easy to blame the other parent. Sometimes there are real reasons to.
But I noticed that every hour I spent rehearsing what they did was an hour I gave away.
My child is half of both of us. When I speak with contempt about the other parent, I am speaking about part of my child too.
This doesn’t mean pretending nothing happened. It means choosing not to let bitterness become my whole personality.
If my child comes back one day, I want them to find a father who is still angry about some things, but not consumed by them.
q: How do you keep resentment from taking over your life?

title: A good day
dek: Good days aren’t betrayal.
body: Yesterday was a good day. I laughed with a friend. I ate a meal I enjoyed. I didn’t check my phone once before lunch.
And then, in the evening, I felt guilty about it.
As if being okay meant I had stopped caring. As if my pain was the only thing still connecting me to my child.
It isn’t. Love doesn’t need suffering to prove it is real.
If you had a good day recently, keep it. You are allowed to. Your child is still in your heart on the good days too.
q: When did you last have a good day, and what made it good?

title: The door stays open
dek: An open door is not the same as an open wound.
body: People sometimes ask how long I will keep the door open. As if there should be a deadline.
I don’t think there is one. But I have learned that keeping the door open doesn’t mean standing in the doorway all day.
I can live my life, build things, see friends, rest. The door is still open while I do.
An open door is a decision, not a vigil. It says: if you ever want to come in, you won’t have to knock twice.
That decision gives me peace in a way that waiting by the door never did.
q: What does keeping the door open look like in your life?

title: For the mothers too
dek: Estrangement doesn’t only happen to fathers.
body: This space is called Dad, Still Here. But we have heard from many mothers too.
Mothers who are judged even more harshly when a child walks away. Mothers who are told it must have been their fault.
The pain is the same pain. The silence is the same silence. The love that has nowhere to go is the same love.
If you are a mother reading this, you are welcome here. Every word on this site is for you as well.
No parent should have to carry this alone.
q: What do you wish people understood about estranged mothers?

title: Still here
dek: Six weeks of entries, and the same promise.
body: When I started writing this, I didn’t know if anyone would read it.
Now I know there are many of us. Fathers and mothers in different towns and countries, checking the same silent phones.
I can’t promise you that your child will come back. I can’t promise you that mine will.
What I can promise is this: I will keep writing. I will keep the door open. I will keep showing up here.
Still here. Still a parent. Still hoping. Thank you for being here too.
q: What keeps you going while you wait?

title: Saying their name out loud
dek: For a long time I stopped saying it. That was a mistake.
body: For a while I couldn’t say my child’s name. Not to friends, not to myself. It caught in my throat.
So I said “my eldest” or “my son” or nothing at all. People stopped asking, and I let them.
Then one evening a friend asked me straight out: “What’s his name?” I said it. The room didn’t fall in.
A name is not a wound. It is a person. Leaving it unsaid felt like agreeing that he had stopped existing, and he hasn’t.
I say it now. Quietly, sometimes. But I say it.
q: Is there a name you have stopped saying out loud?

title: The school photo I never got
dek: Every fall the picture-day envelopes go home. None of the photos come to me.
body: Picture day is coming up at schools all over the country. Kids in their best shirts, hair combed flat for once, envelopes going home in backpacks.
I have four children. I don’t have a recent school photo of any of them.
That is a hard sentence to write. It is harder to live with. Other dads have a row of them on the fridge, a little older every September. Mine stops more than five years ago.

I used to tell myself it was a small thing. A photo is just paper. But it isn’t really about the paper. A school photo is how a parent watches a child grow without being in the room. It is proof that someone thought you should see.

When I don’t get one, I fill the gap myself. I try to picture what my children look like now. My oldest is sixteen. He was a boy the last time I saw him properly. My daughter is fourteen. My two youngest are ten and seven, and the faces I carry of them are faces they don’t have anymore.
I know my picture is wrong. I keep it anyway, because it is all I have, and because I would rather hold a wrong picture than none.
I have learned not to pretend I don’t want to know. For a long time I acted like it didn’t matter, because wanting something you can’t have feels weak. It isn’t weak. It is what a father feels.
So if a photo ever comes, it goes on the fridge. Right in the middle, where I will see it every morning.

There is also a quieter worry underneath it. If I passed my children on the street, would I know them? I think I would. I hope I would. But five years changes a child’s face more than it changes an adult’s, and that thought sits with me longer than I would like.
If you are missing the school photos too, you are not being sentimental. You are being a parent who still wants to see.
q: Is there a picture of your children you wish you had?

title: Why I never changed my number
dek: Same phone number for years. It isn’t an accident.
body: I have changed phones more than once since my children and I lost regular contact. I have never changed the number.
People have suggested it. A fresh start, fewer spam calls, a clean break. I understand why. A number can feel like a door that only ever opens one way.

But it is the number my children know. Some of them were very young the last time we spoke, and I don’t know what they remember. My oldest might remember it. One day the others might find it written down somewhere, or ask for it.

I think about that more than I admit. My son is sixteen now. In a couple of years he will be old enough to decide for himself who he calls. My daughter is not far behind him. When that day comes, I want the number to work. I want it to ring a phone that I answer.
So I keep paying the bill. I keep the voicemail greeting plain and kind. I don’t let the account lapse, even in the months when money is tight.

It is a small thing. Maybe a pointless one. But it is one of the few things I can do that asks nothing of anyone. It doesn’t pressure my children. It doesn’t go around their mom. It just stays there, steady, like a light left on.
Staying reachable doesn’t have to be dramatic. Sometimes it is just not moving.

Sometimes I check the voicemail and there is nothing but a dentist reminder or a robocall. I delete them and feel a small flicker of disappointment every time, which tells me I am still hoping. I have decided that is all right. Hope that costs nothing but a phone bill is hope I can afford.
If you are keeping something the same just in case, you are not foolish. You are keeping a promise nobody else can see.
q: What do you keep the same, just in case?

title: The bad guy in someone else’s story
dek: I may be the villain in the version my children carry. I’ve had to make room for that.
body: I have had to accept something that took me years to say out loud. In the story my children carry about our family, I may be the bad guy.

I don’t know exactly what they have been told, or what they have come to believe on their own. Children make sense of a broken family however they can. When one parent is in the house and the other isn’t, the absent one is easy to fill in.
Everything in me wants to argue. To set out the context, explain what really happened, correct the record. For a long time I did that in my head every night.
It never changed anything. You can’t argue a child out of a story from the outside. And they are children. Sixteen, fourteen, ten and seven. It isn’t their job to be fair to me.

So I am trying to hold two things at once. I can believe I have been misunderstood. I can also admit I got things wrong. Both can be true, and pretending only one of them is true doesn’t help my children.
I won’t speak badly about their mom. Whatever has happened between the adults, she is their mother, and they love her. If I make them choose, I lose either way.
What I can do is be someone who doesn’t match the villain. Steady. Kind. Reachable. If they ever come looking, I want them to find a different man from the one they were afraid of.

There is a kind of freedom in letting go of the argument. When I stopped rehearsing my defense, I had room to think about my children as people again, instead of as a jury I had to win over. They are not my audience. They are my kids, and they are allowed to see things their own way for now.
If you are the bad guy in someone else’s story, you don’t have to win the argument. You just have to keep being who you really are.
q: Have you had to make peace with being misunderstood?

title: Four birthdays a year
dek: Four dates on the calendar that I mark quietly, every year.
body: I have four children, so there are four birthdays a year that I mark on my own.
Some fathers dread one day. I have four, spread through the year like stones in a path. Just as I recover from one, the next is coming.
I know each date without looking. I know how old each of them is turning. Seventeen soon, for my oldest. Fifteen. Eleven. Eight. I say the numbers out loud sometimes, because they keep surprising me.
For the first couple of years I tried to ignore the days. Go to work, stay busy, get to bed. It didn’t work. The day found me anyway, usually in the afternoon, when I stopped moving.

Now I do the opposite. I plan for each birthday a few weeks ahead. I keep the day a little gentler than usual. I think about who that child was the last time I saw them, and I let myself wonder who they are becoming.
I don’t throw a party for someone who isn’t there. I just refuse to pretend it is an ordinary day, because it isn’t. One of my children is a year older, and I am their father, and that matters.
There is a strange comfort in it, too. Four birthdays means four times a year I get to remember out loud that they exist and that I love them.

I also try to think about what each of them might be like at this new age. Not inventing a life for them, just wondering. What does a seventeen-year-old care about? What worries a fifteen-year-old? Wondering keeps me pointed at who they are now, rather than stuck on who they were.
If a birthday is coming for a child you can’t reach, plan for it now. You don’t have to get through it by pretending.
q: How do you handle your children’s birthdays?

title: Doing the math on their ages
dek: Five years is a number. It means something different for each of my children.
body: Sometimes I do the math, even though I know it will hurt.
It has been more than five years since I had regular contact with my children. Five years is just a number until you subtract it from their ages.

My oldest is sixteen. He was around eleven the last time things were normal. That means I missed the whole of middle school with him. His voice has almost certainly changed. He might be taller than me.
My daughter is fourteen. She was around nine. I missed the years when girls change so fast you blink and they are different people.
My son who is ten was around five. He may only remember me in pieces now.
My youngest is seven. He was barely two. If I am honest, he may not remember me at all.
That last one is the hardest. For my older children I am at least a memory, even a complicated one. For my youngest I may be a name, or a story someone told him.

I used to do this math as a kind of punishment. Look at everything you’ve lost. I don’t do it that way anymore. Now I do it to remember that each of my children is living a different version of this, at a different age, with a different understanding.
If any of them ever come back, they won’t come back as the children I remember. I want to be ready to meet who they actually are.

The math also tells me something hopeful, if I let it. My oldest is closer to adulthood than to childhood now. The years that took him further away are also the years that are slowly giving him his own voice. One day the numbers will work the other way.
If you have been doing the same math, be gentle with yourself. The numbers are real. So is your love.
q: How old were your children when the distance began?

title: What I’m missing this fall
dek: Football games, school concerts, first days. I imagine all of it.
body: Fall used to be my favorite time of year. Now it is the season I notice what I am missing most.
Somewhere, my children are in the middle of a school year I know nothing about. New teachers. New friends. A locker combination. Homework they are probably leaving until the last minute.

I imagine a lot of it. I don’t know if my oldest plays a sport or plays an instrument or neither. I don’t know if my daughter has a best friend this year, or if she’s going through the kind of falling out that feels like the end of the world at fourteen. I don’t know what costume the younger two want for Halloween.
I try not to invent too much. It is tempting to build a whole life for them in my head, and then grieve the life I invented. That isn’t fair to them or to me.
So I let myself wonder without pretending to know. I wonder if they are happy. I wonder if they are being treated kindly at school. I wonder who they talk to when something goes wrong.
And then I go back to my own fall. Raking leaves. Watching a game. Doing the small things I can still do.
Missing your kids is not one big feeling. It is a hundred small ones, scattered through a season. Football on a Friday night. A school bus going past. A kid in a store holding a dad’s hand.

Some nights I drive past a high school stadium with the lights on and the crowd noise drifting over the parking lot. I don’t stop. I just slow down for a second and think: one of mine is the right age for this. Then I keep driving, and I let that be enough.
If this fall is full of small aches for you too, you are not overreacting. You are noticing, and noticing is a kind of love.
q: What part of this season makes you miss your children most?

title: When the other parent limits contact
dek: I won’t blame their mom. I also won’t pretend this is how I wanted it.
body: There is no easy way to write about this, so I will say it plainly. Contact with my children is limited by their mom.

I am not going to tell her side of it. I don’t think I could do it fairly, and it isn’t mine to tell. I am not going to blame her here, either. She is my children’s mother. They love her, and they need her.
What I can tell is my side, which is mostly what it feels like to be a father on the outside of his children’s lives.
It feels like waiting at a door you aren’t allowed to knock on. You can see the light on inside. You know they are in there. You can’t go in, and you can’t leave.
For a while I spent most of my energy being angry. Some of that anger was fair. Most of it went nowhere and burned me up from the inside.

These days I try to put that energy somewhere it can do some good. I keep my own life steady. I stay reachable. I write. I do what I can through the proper channels, calmly. I don’t say a word against their mom where it could ever reach my children.
I don’t know if that will change anything. It might not. But I want my children to grow up and find out that their father was never the one who made things worse.

I have also had to learn patience with a process that doesn’t move at the speed of a father’s heart. Paperwork, schedules, waiting for answers that take months. It would be easy to let that wear me down. I try to treat it as part of the work of staying in my children’s lives, even from a distance.
If the other parent limits your contact too, you are allowed to grieve it. Just try not to let the grief turn into something your children would have to carry.
q: How do you protect your children from the conflict between the adults?

title: Five years
dek: Half a decade without my children in my everyday life.
body: It has been more than five years now. Half a decade.
When it started, I thought it would be weeks. Then I thought months. Somewhere along the way I stopped predicting, because every prediction was wrong and every wrong one hurt.
Five years is long enough for everything to change. My children have moved up through grades and schools. They have had birthdays and holidays and ordinary Tuesdays, hundreds of them, without me.
It is also long enough for me to change. I am not the same man I was when this began. I hope I am a better one. I am certainly a quieter one.
People sometimes ask how I’m still standing. Honestly, some days I’m not. Some days I barely make it to the evening. But most days I do, and I have learned that getting through a day is not nothing.

Here is what five years has taught me. Love doesn’t wear out from not being used. I thought it might. I thought it would fade the way a voice fades in memory. It hasn’t. If anything it has gotten steadier, less frantic, more patient.
I don’t know what the next five years will bring. My oldest will be an adult. My youngest will be twelve. Everything might change, or nothing might.
Either way I will still be here, still their father, still keeping the door open.

I have also stopped measuring the years only in loss. Five years of keeping my word. Five years of not giving up. Five years of choosing, every morning, to be a father who stays. Those things count too, even if nobody sees them but me.
Some days I still catch myself thinking it will all be fixed by next spring. I let the thought come and go. I don’t need a deadline to keep going.
If you are counting years too, you are not alone in it. Plenty of us are counting quietly.
q: How long has it been for you, and what has the time taught you?

title: What I would want them to know
dek: If my children read one thing I wrote, this is what I would want it to say.
body: I think a lot about what I would want my children to know, if they ever read any of this.

Not the whole story. Not my side of every argument. They are children, and they don’t need to carry the adults’ version of events. If they want it one day, I will answer their questions honestly. Until then, it can wait.
What I would want them to know is simpler than that.
That I never stopped being their father. Not for one day, not even on the days I could barely get out of bed.
That I have thought about each of them by name, every single day, for more than five years.
That none of this was their fault. Children sometimes believe they caused the trouble between the adults. They didn’t. Not one of them, not in any way.
That I am not angry with them. Whatever they have heard, whatever they believe right now, there is nothing they need to apologize for.
That my door is open, and it will stay open, without conditions. They don’t have to explain anything, prove anything, or choose between anyone.
And that I hope they are happy. I hope people are kind to them. I hope they laugh a lot.
I write this down because some days it helps me remember what really matters underneath all the hurt.

I keep a version of this written down where I can find it. On bad days I read it back, and it reminds me that underneath the anger and the waiting, the message has never really changed. It is the same few sentences, over and over. I love you. It wasn’t your fault. I’m here.
If you have something you would want your children to know, it might be worth writing it down too. Even if nobody reads it yet.
q: What is the one thing you would want your children to know?

title: “Do you have kids?”
dek: The most ordinary question in the world, and the hardest one to answer.
kw: how to answer do you have kids when estranged
body: Somebody asks it at a cookout, a work event, the barber shop. “Do you have kids?” It is the most normal question in the world.
For a long time I didn’t know what to say.
If I said no, I felt like I was erasing my own children. Four of them, real and alive, growing up somewhere. Saying no felt like a betrayal.

If I said yes, the next question was always coming. How old? What are they into? Did you see the game with them? And then I was either lying or explaining far more than a stranger at a cookout wants to hear.
So for years I changed the subject. I got good at it. Too good, probably.
Now I say this. “I have four. Sixteen, fourteen, ten and seven. We’re not in touch right now.”
Most people nod and move on. A few look awkward. And every so often, someone goes quiet and then says, “Me too.”
That surprised me more than anything. There are more of us than you would think. Standing at the same parties, holding the same paper plates, answering the same question with the same careful words.
You don’t owe anyone the whole story. You don’t have to explain whose fault it is or what happened. But you are allowed to say yes. They are your children. You are allowed to claim them out loud.

I have also had to get comfortable with the silence that sometimes follows. Not everyone knows what to say, and that is fine. I don’t need them to fix it. Saying the true answer out loud, in an ordinary place, is something I do for myself as much as for anyone listening.
If you have been dodging this question, try the short honest version next time. You might find someone who understands.
q: How do you answer when someone asks if you have children?

title: Staying the dad they can come back to
dek: If my children come looking one day, I want them to find me well.
body: There was a stretch when I let a lot of things slide. Sleep. Meals. Doctor’s appointments. What was the point, when the people I was doing it for weren’t there to see?
Then I started thinking about it differently.

My oldest is sixteen. In a couple of years, he will be old enough to make his own choices about who he sees. My daughter will be right behind him. My youngest two have a while to go, but that day will come for them too.
When any of them come looking, if they come looking, which version of me will they find?
I don’t want it to be a man who gave up. I don’t want them to find someone bitter, or unwell, or so lost in the past that there is no room for who they are now.
So I started small. Eating properly. Getting outside. Booking the checkup I had been avoiding. Being honest with a friend about how I really was.
None of it guarantees anything. My children might not come back for years, or at all. But it means that whatever happens, I am here, and in decent shape to be here.
It is also the only part of this that is fully in my hands. I can’t change the past. I can’t control what my children are told or what they decide. I can decide what kind of man is waiting.
Looking after yourself is not moving on. It is getting ready.

I think about the practical things, too. A spare bed if they ever need one. A life with enough room in it for four kids to walk back into. Not a shrine, just space. Being ready doesn’t mean waiting in a chair by the window. It means building a life they could fit into.
If you have let things slide too, pick one small thing this week. Do it for the dad they might come back to.
q: What is one small thing you could do for yourself this week?

title: Halloween without my kids
dek: Four costumes I won’t see this year.
body: Halloween is coming. The stores have been full of costumes since September.

Somewhere, my children are deciding what to be this year. Or at least the younger ones are. At sixteen and fourteen, my oldest two might think they are too old for it, or they might be going to a party, or handing out candy at the door. I don’t know.

My two youngest are ten and seven. Prime trick-or-treating age. I imagine them working out their costumes, arguing over who gets which candy at the end of the night. I don’t know if that is what happens. I let myself picture it anyway.
Holidays without your kids have a particular weight. The whole neighborhood turns into a celebration of families. Kids in costumes, parents with flashlights, porches lit up and waiting.
I have learned to plan for it rather than be ambushed by it.

I buy candy and answer the door. I like seeing the kids in their costumes, even when it aches a little. It reminds me that childhood is still happening, for my children too, even if I am not there to see it.
Later, when the porch light is off, I let myself feel it. I don’t pretend it is fine. I just let the evening end gently.
The holidays will keep coming. Thanksgiving next, then Christmas. I would rather meet each one with a plan than spend weeks dreading it.

I also remember that my children are having their own version of this night. Whatever they feel about me, they are still kids on Halloween, and I want it to be a good one for them. That is the strange thing about loving someone from far away. You end up hoping hardest for the nights you won’t be part of.
If Halloween is hard for you this year, you are not the only parent with the porch light on and an empty feeling inside.
q: How do you get through the holidays when your children aren’t with you?

title: Questions I would ask my children
dek: Four kids, four different lists. I keep adding to them.
body: I keep a list in my head of questions I would ask my children if I got the chance. Not big questions. Small ones.
For my oldest, who is sixteen: What music are you listening to? Are you learning to drive? Who do you go to when something goes wrong?
For my daughter, who is fourteen: Who is your best friend this year? What makes you laugh? What do you want to be, today, even if it changes next week?
For my son who is ten: What are you really good at? What is the best thing that happened at school this month?
For my youngest, who is seven: What is your favorite thing in the whole world right now? I would let him talk as long as he wanted.

I notice that none of my questions are about me. I don’t want to ask if they think about me, or what they have been told, or whether they are angry. Those questions are for me, not for them. If we ever sit down together, the first job is to listen.

The lists change as they get older. The questions I would have asked a two-year-old don’t fit a seven-year-old anymore. Updating them is one of the ways I try to keep up with who my children are becoming, instead of who they were.

Some days it feels a little foolish, keeping lists for conversations that might not happen. But it keeps me pointed in the right direction. Toward curiosity instead of grievance. Toward them instead of the past.
Missing my children isn’t only about what I lost. It is also about everything I still want to know.

I also try to imagine what they might ask me. Why I wasn’t there. Whether I still think about them. I don’t have perfect answers, but I want my first answer to be honest and short: I never stopped loving you.
If you keep a list like this too, you are not wasting your time. You are getting ready to listen.
q: What would you ask your children first, if you could?

title: When friends talk about their kids
dek: Their stories are ordinary. That’s exactly what makes them hard to hear.
body: My friends talk about their kids. Of course they do. It is what parents do.
A soccer game. A bad report card. A teenager who won’t get off his phone. A little one who refuses to wear anything but one pair of shoes.
Most of the time I am glad to listen. These are good people, and their kids matter to me because they matter to them.

But sometimes the ordinary stories land hard. Not because anything sad happened in them. Because nothing did. Just normal family life, the kind I used to have, the kind my children are living somewhere without me.

For a while I avoided those conversations. I’d change the subject or find a reason to leave. That made me lonelier. Being an estranged father is isolating enough without shutting out the people who are trying to stay close.

So now I try to stay. And when it gets too much, I try to be honest in a small way. “I love hearing this. It’s also a bit hard for me.” Most friends can hold both. A few have even started asking about my kids, gently, which I didn’t expect and didn’t know I needed.

I have also learned that my friends often don’t know what to say to me. They worry that talking about their kids will hurt, so they stop. That silence can feel worse than the stories. Telling them it is okay to talk, and okay to ask, has helped all of us.
The loneliness doesn’t disappear. But it shrinks a little when the people around you know the truth.

There is one more thing I have noticed. When a friend shares something hard about their own kids, a sick child or a teenager in trouble, I find I can be there for them in a way I couldn’t before. Missing my own children has made me a better listener for everyone else’s.
If you have been pulling away from friends with kids, you don’t have to. You can stay in the room and still be honest about how it feels.
q: How do you handle it when friends talk about their children?

title: The evenings are the hardest
dek: The day keeps me busy. The evening doesn’t.
body: If you asked me what time of day is hardest, I wouldn’t say mornings, or birthdays, or holidays. I would say ordinary evenings.
During the day there is work, errands, people, noise. Something always needs doing. The missing is there, but it stays in the background.

Then the evening comes. The house gets quiet. That is when I think about my children most. What they are having for dinner. Whether the younger two are fighting over the bath. Whether my oldest is up in his room with the door closed, the way teenagers are.
For a long time I just let the evenings happen to me. I would sit with the TV on and not watch it, and go to bed late, and wake up tired.

Coping with estrangement, for me, has mostly meant building a little structure around those hours. Nothing dramatic. A walk after dinner when the weather allows. A call to someone on certain nights of the week. Reading instead of scrolling. Going to bed at a sensible time, even when my mind wants to stay up and go over everything again.
Some nights none of that works and I just have to get through it. I have stopped treating those nights as failures. They are part of it.
What helps most is knowing the feeling will pass by morning. It always has. The evening is long, but it ends.
I don’t think the evenings will ever be easy while my children are somewhere else. But they can be gentler than they were.

I have also stopped going over old conversations in the evening. That used to be my habit, replaying what was said years ago and rewriting it. It never changed anything. Now, when I notice I’m doing it, I get up and do something with my hands instead.
If your evenings are the hardest part too, start with one small thing to give them shape. You don’t have to fix the whole night.
q: What helps you get through the evenings?

title: Keeping the adults’ business out of it
dek: Whatever happens between the grown-ups, my children shouldn’t have to carry it.
body: There is one rule I try never to break. My children should not have to carry what happened between the adults.
Their mom limits contact. I have feelings about that, and some of them are not kind. I won’t pretend otherwise. But those feelings are mine to deal with. They don’t belong in my children’s lives.
Kids in the middle of family conflict often feel like they have to pick a side. They feel guilty for loving one parent in front of the other. I don’t want to add to that, not even from a distance.

So I am careful. I don’t write anything here that could make my children feel they have to defend their mom, or defend me. I don’t share the details of what happened, and I don’t put blame on anyone in public. If my children ever read this blog, I want them to find a father who missed them, not a father who was keeping score.

It isn’t always easy. Some days I want to explain myself so badly it feels physical. I want people to know my side. But I have come to believe that the most loving thing I can do is let my children be children, and keep the adult business with the adults.
That doesn’t mean pretending everything is fine. It means choosing where the hard things go. To a friend. To a counselor. To my own journal. Not to my kids.
If they ask me one day what happened, I will answer honestly, at a level that fits their age. Until then, they deserve a childhood without a war in it.

There is a practical side to this too. I keep any communication with their mom short, polite, and about the children. I read anything I write twice before I send it. I would rather be boring and calm than right and angry.
If you are in a conflict with your children’s other parent, it might be the hardest discipline there is. It is also one of the kindest.
q: How do you keep your children out of the conflict between the adults?

title: My oldest is sixteen
dek: He was a boy the last time things were normal. Now he’s nearly a man.
body: My oldest is sixteen now. I say it out loud sometimes, because it still surprises me.
He was around eleven when regular contact ended. Eleven-year-olds still hold your hand in a parking lot, sometimes. Sixteen-year-olds don’t.

I think about everything that happens between eleven and sixteen. Middle school. The start of high school. A voice that cracks and then drops. A growth spurt that makes all his clothes too small in one summer. Maybe a first crush. Maybe learning to drive.
I don’t know which of those things have happened. I don’t want to pretend I do.

Being estranged from a teenage son has a particular ache. These are the years when a boy works out what kind of man he wants to be. I always thought I would be there for that, not lecturing, just around. Someone to watch, to argue with, to come back to.

I am not there. That is the truth. But I have also realized that he is getting close to the age where he gets to make more of his own choices. In a couple of years, he will be an adult. What he decides then will be up to him.
I want him to know, if he ever wonders, that I never stopped being his dad. That my number is the same. That there is nothing he needs to explain or apologize for.
I also want to be honest with myself. He may not come looking. If he does, he will come as a young man with his own view of things, and I will need to listen far more than I talk.
Sometimes I wonder what he looks like now, and whether he got my height or his mom’s. It is a small question. It still catches me off guard how much I want the answer.
If you have a teenager you can’t reach, the distance is real. So is the fact that they are growing toward their own choices.
q: What do you hope your teenager knows about you?

title: Not knowing if they’re okay
dek: The hardest question isn’t “why.” It’s “are they all right?”
body: People assume the hardest question for an estranged father is “why.” For me it isn’t. The hardest question is “are they okay?”
Are they healthy? Are they sleeping well? Is anyone being unkind to them at school? Are they happy, most days?

Normally a parent gets a hundred small answers to those questions every week. A kid who comes home cheerful. A kid who slams a door. A kid who eats everything in the fridge. You learn to read them without thinking.
I don’t get those answers. So the worry has nowhere to land. It just circles.
For a while I let my imagination fill the gap, and my imagination is not kind at two in the morning. It invents the worst. That doesn’t help my children and it doesn’t help me.

What helps is reminding myself of what I do know. My children have their mom. They have school, teachers, and other people in their lives. Most days, for most kids, are ordinary. There is a good chance they are fine, and that their ordinary days are full of ordinary things.

I also remind myself that worry is a form of love. It means I still care about the details of their lives, even the ones I can’t see. I don’t want to stop caring. I just want to stop letting the worry run the night.
So I try to turn it into something steadier. A hope, said quietly, that they are safe and happy. Then I put it down for the night.

There is also comfort in knowing that most of what keeps children safe and happy doesn’t require me. Good teachers. Friends. A routine. A parent who loves them at home. I can hope those things are there for them, and most likely they are.
If you are worried about your children and can’t reach them, you are not overreacting. You are a parent without the usual answers. Be gentle with yourself.
q: How do you handle the worry when you can’t check on your children?

title: Holding on to who they were
dek: The children I remember are real. They are also not who my children are now.
body: I have memories of my children that I go back to often. Small ones. A laugh. A way of standing. The weight of a sleeping child on my shoulder.
Those children were real. That matters. Nothing that has happened since can make those years not have happened.

But I have had to admit something hard. The children I remember are not exactly the children who exist now. My oldest is not the boy in my memory anymore. My youngest was so small that my memory of him is almost a different person.

There is a name for this kind of grief. People call it grieving a living child, or ambiguous loss. Your children are alive and well, as far as you know, and you are still grieving. Not their life. Your place in it.
For a long time I didn’t know if I was allowed to call it grief. Nobody died. There was no funeral. People sometimes treat it as something you should just get over.
I don’t think you get over it. I think you learn to carry it. And part of carrying it, for me, is holding the old memories gently without mistaking them for the present.

I keep the memories. I take them out when I need them. Then I put them back, and I remind myself that my children have kept growing, the way they were supposed to. That is a good thing, even if I wasn’t there for it.

Some days I write the memories down, just so they don’t fade. Not to live in them. To have them somewhere safe, the way you keep a photo in a drawer. I can open the drawer when I need to and close it when I don’t.
If you are grieving children who are still living, your grief is real. You don’t need anyone’s permission to feel it.
q: What memory of your children do you hold on to most?

title: Letting them be who they are now
dek: If we ever meet again, I want to meet the people they’ve become.
body: Yesterday I wrote about holding on to who my children were. Today I want to write about letting them be who they are now.

If I am ever lucky enough to see my children again, I won’t be meeting the kids from my memories. I will be meeting a sixteen-year-old, a fourteen-year-old, a ten-year-old and a seven-year-old, or older by then. People with their own opinions, habits, and ways of seeing the world.
They may not like the same things. They may not want to be called the old nicknames. They may remember things differently from me, or not remember some things at all.

Reconnecting with estranged children, from what I understand, often goes wrong when the parent tries to pick up exactly where they left off. As if the years in between didn’t count. But those years are the whole of my children’s recent lives. They count more than anything.
So I am trying to get ready in a different way. Less “here is who you were.” More “tell me who you are.”
That means being ready to hear things I might not like. Ready to be corrected. Ready to be patient if they are cautious, or quiet, or angry. Ready to let them set the pace.

It also means I have to let go of some of my own picture of how it would go. The big emotional reunion I sometimes imagined is probably not what happens. If anything happens, it will likely be small, careful, and slow. That is okay. Small and real is better than big and imagined.

There is a kind of hope in this, too. Children who grow up get the chance to make their own decisions. The people my children are becoming will one day decide for themselves who they want in their lives. I want to be ready to meet them as equals, with respect.
If you hope to reconnect one day, start practicing curiosity now. The person who comes back will be someone new.
q: What would you want to learn about your children as they are now?

title: Why I write this
dek: Every day, for parents who are waiting too.
body: I get asked sometimes why I write this blog. Why I put something so private out where anyone can read it.
The honest answer is that I didn’t know where else to put it.

After more than five years without regular contact with my four children, I had a lot of thoughts that had nowhere to go. Some were too heavy for my friends. Some were too ordinary for a counselor. Most of them just sat in me and went around in circles.
Writing them down every day helped. It turned the circles into sentences. Once something is a sentence, I can look at it, and sometimes I can put it down.

I also write because when I first went looking for anything about fathers in my situation, I found very little. There were articles, and studies, and advice. There weren’t many dads just saying what it was like. I wanted to read that, so I started writing it.

I am careful about what I share. I don’t name my children. I don’t tell the adults’ side of the story, and I won’t blame their mom. This blog is about what it is like to be a father on the outside, not a case I am trying to make.
And I write because of you. Every so often someone sends a message through the site saying they read an entry and felt less alone. That is the best thing that has come out of any of this.
I will keep writing, every day, for as long as it helps someone.

Writing has also changed me. It has made me slower to anger and quicker to notice what I am actually feeling. Some entries I write in ten minutes. Some take a whole evening. Every one of them has helped me understand this a little better.
If you have been carrying this on your own, you are welcome here. You don’t have to say anything. You can just read.
q: What has helped you feel less alone in this?

title: When the clocks fall back
dek: Daylight saving ends tonight. The long dark evenings start tomorrow.
body: The clocks fall back tonight. Tomorrow it will be dark by dinnertime, and it will stay that way until spring.

For a lot of parents in my situation, this is when the year gets harder. Shorter days mean longer evenings. Longer evenings mean more time inside with your own thoughts. And the holidays are right around the corner, which brings its own weight.
I used to be ambushed by it every year. I would notice in December that I had been sinking since November, and wonder why.
Now I try to plan for it. Seasonal loneliness is real, and it gets worse when you are already missing your children. Knowing that ahead of time helps.

So this week I am putting a few things in place. Some light in the evenings. Plans with people on the nights I know are hardest. Getting outside in daylight, even for a few minutes, especially on weekends. Paying attention to my sleep, because everything feels worse when I am tired.
I am also giving myself permission to have a hard winter if it turns out that way. Planning for it doesn’t mean I have to be fine. It just means I am not facing it unprepared.

If you notice yourself sinking in the coming weeks, it might not be a personal failing. It might be the season, landing on top of something that is already heavy. Talk to someone if it gets to be too much. Your doctor counts. A friend counts.
The dark months are long, but they end. Spring comes back, the same as it always does.

One more thing I have learned. The first week after the clocks change is usually the worst. My body takes a while to adjust, and my mood follows. Knowing that, I try not to make big decisions or send important messages that week.
If you are dreading the winter, start building a little support around it now. You don’t have to brace for it alone.
q: What helps you get through the darker months?

title: A father to four, from far away
dek: Four children, four ages, four different kinds of missing.
kw: being a father from a distance
body: Being a father to four children is a lot of things. Being a father to four children from far away is its own kind of work.
People sometimes talk about estrangement as if it were one loss. For me it is four. Each of my children is a different person, at a different age, and I miss each of them differently.
With my oldest, at sixteen, I miss the conversations we might be having now. The arguments, even. The chance to be someone he could come to as he works out his life.
With my daughter, at fourteen, I miss being around while she becomes herself. I worry about whether she knows how proud of her I would be.
With my son who is ten, I miss the age when kids still want you to watch everything they do.
With my youngest, at seven, I miss almost his whole childhood so far. That one is the hardest to think about for long.

Being a father from a distance means I can’t do most of what fathers do. I can’t drive them to practice or help with homework or sit at the end of the bed when someone is sick. What I can do is smaller, but it is not nothing.

I can keep my number the same. I can stay well. I can keep my word about not speaking badly of their mom. I can keep writing down what I would want them to know, so it is there if they ever look. And I can keep loving each of them, specifically, by name, every day.

Some nights I think about each of them in turn before I sleep. Just a moment for each one, in order of age. It is not a ritual anyone else would notice. It keeps all four of them close in a way that is entirely mine.
If you are a parent to several children you can’t reach, it is okay to miss each one in their own way. They are not one loss. They are each their own person.
q: How do you hold on to each of your children as individuals?

title: Getting ready for Thanksgiving
dek: Three weeks out. I’m planning for it now, on purpose.
body: Thanksgiving is about three weeks away. The grocery stores are already stacking pumpkin pie filling by the door.

For years I didn’t plan for it. I would let it arrive, and then feel blindsided by how much it hurt. A holiday built around family at one table is a hard day when your children are at a different one.
This year I am starting early, on purpose.
First, I am deciding where I will be. Being alone on Thanksgiving is sometimes the right choice, but I want it to be a choice, not something that happens to me because I didn’t make a plan.

Second, I am thinking about what I want from the day. Maybe it is a quiet meal with someone who knows my situation and won’t make me explain. Maybe it is being useful somewhere, helping serve a meal for people who need one. Maybe it is a long walk in the morning before anything else.

Third, I am deciding how I want to mark my children’s absence. I don’t want to pretend they don’t exist. I also don’t want the whole day to be about what is missing. Something small feels right. A moment, a sentence, a thought for each of them. Then I will let the day carry on.
And last, I am being honest that it might still be hard. A plan doesn’t make the feeling go away. It just means I won’t be facing it with nothing to hold on to.

Thanksgiving without my children will never be what I want. But it can still have some gratitude in it. For the years I had with them. For the people around me now. For the fact that they are out there, growing up.

I will probably also write here that day. Not a long entry. Just something for the other parents who will be setting a table without their children and trying to find something to be thankful for anyway.
If you are dreading the holidays, start your plan this week. Even a small one helps.
q: What is one thing you could plan now to make Thanksgiving gentler?
